title: Supplier Divorce Protection: Tool Census and Overrun Forensics
one_liner: When a US manufacturer leaves a Chinese contract manufacturer, we find out which molds and dies it really owns, and prove whether the ex-supplier is still running them off the books.
customer: US OEMs and PE-owned manufacturers ($50M-$500M revenue) that moved or are moving injection-molded, die-cast, stamped or extruded product out of China within the last 24 months, and hold $200k-$5M of tooling there. The buyer is the COO or VP Supply Chain, with General Counsel as co-signer. General counsel and brand-protection managers are the second buyer.
problem: Most small and mid-size OEMs cannot say which tools they own, where they physically sit, or what condition they are in. The paper trail is a PO line item from 2016 and a WeChat thread. When the relationship ends, the supplier slow-walks tool release, demands storage or release fees, and sometimes runs overruns on your tooling on a third shift and sells them to distributors and marketplaces at a discount. You then compete against your own product, and lawyers cannot help because nobody can prove which tool made which part.
solution: Three stacked products. (1) Tool Census: a local partner audits each supplier on video and in person, laser-tags every tool with a serial, records its condition and appraised value, and captures a macro-photo 'fingerprint' library of each cavity (gate vestige, ejector-pin witness marks, texture flaws, parting-line signature). (2) Overrun Watch: monitor Amazon, Alibaba, 1688, Temu, eBay and Walmart Marketplace for look-alike parts, buy samples, and match them to cavity fingerprints, date wheels and lot codes with computer-vision-assisted forensics. That yields evidence packs for marketplace takedowns, CBP IPR recordation, or counsel. (3) Tool Extraction: negotiate release, handle Chinese export paperwork and freight, and re-qualify the tool in Ohio.
why_now: The Reshoring Initiative's 2026 survey shows 36% of OEMs reshored this year, up from 29%. The 2025 tariff whiplash ended a lot of Chinese supplier relationships, and the Feb 2026 Supreme Court IEEPA ruling is now churning sourcing decisions again, so the number of messy breakups is at a peak. Cheap macro-imaging and vision models make tool-mark matching, previously an expensive forensic-lab exercise, feasible at SMB prices.
revenue_model: Tool Census at $6k-$15k per supplier site. Overrun Watch at $2k-$5k per month per product family. Forensic evidence pack at $3k-$8k per case. Extraction at 8-12% of appraised tool value plus pass-through freight. Expected first-year ACV per client is $40k-$120k.
non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think IP loss in China means someone copies your design. Insiders know the far bigger leak is your own paid-for tool running unrecorded shifts, and that every cavity is a physical fingerprint the supplier cannot deny. Ownership of the tooling is the real leverage in any break-up, and almost nobody documents it until the day they need it.
first_30_days: Skip China operations at first. Sell a remote $2,500 'Marketplace Overrun Audit': buy 10 units of the client's product from 1688, Alibaba and Temu, compare them to the golden sample and lot codes, and deliver a one-page verdict. Sign 3 design partners through Ohio plant-manager and Reshoring Initiative networks, and line up a Dongguan or Ningbo audit contractor by referral. Book a one-hour consult with an IP litigator who will white-label the evidence-pack format.

title: Insurer-Proof Watch Service for Inherited Houses
one_liner: A subscription that keeps a parent's empty house insured during probate by producing the dated inspection log insurers require, plus leak sensors and mail and utility handling.
customer: Adult children and executors managing a deceased or institutionalized parent's home from another city ($149-$249/month), reached through probate attorneys, realtors, senior move managers and estate-sale companies.
problem: Standard homeowner policies typically stop covering vandalism, theft and most water damage after 30-60 days of vacancy. Repairs from an undetected burst pipe run $10,000-$70,000 and claims have been denied at $60,000. Dedicated vacant-home policies cost roughly 25-60% more. Probate can bar sale for 9-18 months, so the house sits empty while heirs pay taxes, insurance and utilities and rarely visit.
solution: Weekly walk-throughs by vetted local checkers (off-duty inspectors, retirees) with timestamped photo and checklist logs in the format carriers accept. Add $30 cellular leak and freeze sensors, mail and utility management, seasonal tasks, and a monthly PDF the executor can hand to the insurer and the probate court. Broker partnerships handle the vacancy endorsement, and the service later hands off to cleanout and sale referrals.
why_now: The great wealth transfer is putting millions of parents' houses into estates. Cellular leak sensors are now $30, gig labor is easy to source, and homeowners carriers are tightening on vacancy as claims costs rise. Executors are increasingly remote adult children.
revenue_model: $149-$249/month subscription for 6-12 months (average lifetime about $1,500-$2,500), plus broker commission on vacancy endorsements and referral fees on cleanout and listing.
non_obvious_insight: Loss-adjuster guidance says the documentation that preserves coverage during vacancy is 'dated inspection photos with visit logs' plus utility and contractor records, so the inspection log itself is the product, and nobody sells it to heirs (https://vectorclaimsolutions.com/vacancy-clause-property-insurance/, which also cites a $60,000 vacancy-clause denial and 50-60% premiums for dedicated vacant policies). Carrying cost and vacancy-insurance friction for heirs is described at https://www.wedgewoodhomes.com/blog/vacant-house-insurance-inherited-home. Reddit was unreachable, so this is drawn from insurance and estate-practice sources describing the recurring 'we inherited Mom's house, now what?' thread pattern in r/AgingParents and r/homeowners.
first_30_days: Choose one metro. Recruit 5 checkers at about $35 per visit and buy 20 sensors. Pitch 15 probate attorneys and senior move managers with a one-page 'keep the house insured during probate' offer at $199/month. Sign 10 customers, verify with 2 carriers or agents that the log satisfies their vacancy conditions, and use that as the sales proof.

title: Bring-Into-Use Satellites for Spectrum Filing Holders
one_liner: Fixed-price rideshare satellites that let holders of valuable spectrum and orbit filings meet ITU hardware milestones instead of losing them.
customer: Telecom ministries and regulators of small and mid-size states (Gulf, Africa, Pacific, Central Asia, Latin America), plus startups that hold NGSO filings but cannot afford a full constellation.
problem: Spectrum and orbit rights are now priced like beachfront (EchoStar's reported $23B sale to AT&T and $17B sale to SpaceX), yet ITU rules still require real hardware in orbit by set deadlines. A holder of paper filings is one missed milestone from losing the asset, and a real constellation costs hundreds of millions.
solution: A standard 6U-12U bus with a software-defined payload configurable to the filed bands, sold as a 'milestone in a box'. The package covers rideshare launch, operations, evidence for the administration and coordination paperwork. Regulatory counsel decides what counts as bringing into use for each filing. Entry product is a filing-health audit built from public ITU data.
why_now: The 2025-26 EchoStar deals reset what spectrum is worth. Rideshare is plentiful (321 orbital launches in 2025 per the briefing). Commercial 6U buses and SDR payloads are off the shelf, and nine-figure rounds at European bus makers show integration capacity is growing. Sovereign space programs are multiplying.
revenue_model: Audit $20-50k. Fixed-price milestone satellite $1.5-4M. Annual retainer of $100-300k for filing maintenance and coordination. Optional success fee when a preserved filing is sold or leased.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders treat filings as paper assets and hardware as optional. The ITU makes hardware the price of keeping the paper, so the scarce thing is cheap, compliant placeholder hardware plus the regulatory playbook. Nobody sells that as a product.
first_30_days: Hire one ex-administration or ITU filing specialist on contract. Scrape public ITU filing data and rank about 100 filings by deadline urgency. Send personalized audits to 50 administrations and startups, and charge for the first five. Collect LOI-backed pre-orders before committing to hardware.

title: Orphan Fleet Depot for Bankrupt-Maker Electric Buses
one_liner: Sustainment-as-a-service for school districts and transit agencies stuck with electric buses whose manufacturer went bankrupt, using the military's orphan-platform playbook (salvaged parts pool, configuration control, depot repair, availability guarantees).
customer: School districts, regional education service agencies and small transit agencies that own buses from failed OEMs (Lion Electric US buses, Proterra, and similar EV truck and bus makers), plus state grant administrators and cooperative-purchasing bodies that want the taxpayer-funded fleets running.
problem: When Lion Electric went through bankruptcy and its new owner voided prior U.S. warranties, districts were left with buses nobody would service. Some sourced parts themselves, some sidelined buses, and some went back to diesel. Proterra's transit business went through a similar handoff. Grant-funded buses that sit idle are a political and audit embarrassment. Dealers cannot fix proprietary battery, inverter and charge-port faults, and there is no parts channel.
solution: Run it like a military orphan-platform sustainment program. (1) Buy the bankruptcy estate's remaining parts, tooling and diagnostics at liquidation. (2) Build a per-VIN configuration database and a reverse-engineered diagnostic library. (3) Stand up a regional depot and a mobile repair van for line-replaceable units: contactors, DC-DC converters, charge ports, battery management modules and pack modules. (4) Buy sidelined orphan buses cheaply as cannibalization donors. (5) Sell a fixed annual sustainment contract per bus that guarantees a morning-route availability rate, backed by a shared spares pool across districts sized with readiness-based sparing math.
why_now: Lion's sale voided U.S. warranties (reported late 2025), so the 2025-26 school year is when the pain became real. The installed base of grant-funded EV buses is large and aging out of warranty, and subsidy rollbacks (the federal commercial clean vehicle credit ended for vehicles acquired after Sept 30, 2025) make further OEM failures likely. The parts estates of failed makers are cheapest to buy right now, before anyone else sees their value.
revenue_model: Annual sustainment contract of roughly $4-8k per bus with an availability guarantee, plus time-and-materials for depot repairs, spares-pool membership fees for districts that want priority access, and salvage and refurbished battery pack sales. Sold through cooperative purchasing vehicles so districts do not each run a bid.
non_obvious_insight: Orphaned does not mean unfixable. In most orphaned fleets, 5-10 recurring line-replaceable units cause most of the downtime. A small shared spares pool plus a configuration-controlled baseline can lift availability from a coin flip to about 90%. The right buyer is not one district's bus garage but a state agency or regional service center pooling many districts, because the sparing math only works at fleet-of-fleets scale. Military sustainers call this the DMSMS problem and solved it by owning the baseline instead of waiting for the OEM.
first_30_days: Build a list of about 20 districts that took Lion or similar deliveries in 2022-24 from press coverage and grant award lists. Offer one district a free 'orphan health check' on a stranded bus using generic diagnostic tools and an EV-experienced transit mechanic. Register as a bidder in the relevant bankruptcy and liquidation processes and ask for the parts inventory lists. Hire 1-2 retired transit or heavy-duty EV technicians. Sign three districts to a per-bus quarterly pilot and use their fault logs to identify the top recurring failure modes.

title: Retirement-in-a-Box for Exiting Appraisers
one_liner: Take the workfile custody, E&O tail worry and direct lender clients off retiring appraisers, then hand the practice to supervised trainees, a bridge the industry has never had.
customer: Certified residential appraisers about 58 and older deciding whether to learn the new UAD 3.6 workflow or quit pay $1,500-2,500 one-time. Successor side: credit unions, community banks and attorneys with direct-relationship orders pay recurring fees. Career-changers (agents, inspectors, adjusters, contractors) become trainees under our supervisors.
problem: An appraisal practice has no sale value. The license is personal and the AMC clients aren't transferable. Retirement is also frightening. USPAP requires workfiles to be retained and retrievable for at least 5 years (longer with litigation). E&O claims can arrive years later, so a costly tail policy is needed. Board complaints and subpoenas don't stop. Meanwhile UAD 3.6 becomes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 with new forms and data, which is pushing veterans to quit rather than relearn. The active workforce has reportedly shrunk from over 90,000 (2016) to about 65,000, and rural counties lose their only appraiser.
solution: (1) Secure digital workfile custody with retrieval, subpoena and board-inquiry response, and a group E&O tail program (brokerage commission). (2) A recorded 3-hour 'local knowledge' interview plus the retiree's adjustment grids and neighborhood boundary notes, packaged into a playbook for the successor. (3) Successor placement: trainees under a certified supervisor of record (the retiree part-time for 12-24 months on a stipend and earn-out, or another certified appraiser), with desk-review and AI QC before signature. (4) The retiree's direct lender clients move to the successor with a personal handoff.
why_now: UAD 3.6 is mandatory for new GSE submissions from Nov 2, 2026. The AQB's second exposure draft (comments closed Aug 30, 2026) proposes removing the college-degree requirement and experience-timeline barriers, which widens the trainee pool. Executive Order 14393 (March 2026) directs regulators to simplify appraiser qualifications and expand alternative valuations. The rural shortage is acute and lenders want reliable local coverage.
revenue_model: $1,800 one-time custody plus transition package, or about $29/month for archive-only. E&O tail brokerage commissions. A 15-25% earn-out on inherited direct-client revenue for 24 months. 20-30% of trainee-produced fee revenue for QC and supervisor-of-record services. Coverage-guarantee contracts with rural credit unions and community banks.
non_obvious_insight: The asset isn't the license. It's about 200 workfiles, 15 direct-client phone numbers and 25 years of local adjustment knowledge, and the real exit barrier is fear of tail liability, not money. Solve the fear and the successor gets clients and know-how at near-zero acquisition cost. VCs assume AI will make appraisers obsolete. The near-term truth is that the supply of human signatures (the liability bearers) is collapsing faster than software replaces them, and whoever owns the signatures and the QC owns the workflow. Supervisors, not trainees, are the scarce resource.
first_30_days: Pull public state board rosters in 3-4 states (for example TX, OH, PA, CO) and filter certified residential appraisers licensed 25+ years. Run a free 'UAD 3.6: adapt or retire' session through local Appraisal Institute chapters and appraiser Facebook groups. Sign 10 retirees to the $1,500 custody plus tail package. Recruit 5 trainees from local agents and inspectors. Hold two credit union lunches to line up the direct-client handoffs.

title: Hospital Back-Office Campuses Become Staff Housing
one_liner: Help nonprofit health systems convert surplus administrative office campuses, emptied by AI scribes and revenue-cycle automation, into staff housing, with the hospital itself as the master-lease credit that makes the conversion financeable.
customer: Nonprofit health-system CFOs and real-estate heads pay a fixed-fee feasibility engagement plus a success fee. Development and lending partners are secondary.
problem: Health systems own large billing, coding and admin campuses just as ambient AI (over 70% of large delivery networks have deployed or piloted scribes) and revenue-cycle automation shrink back-office headcount. Medicaid work requirements threaten 12.5-14.2% operating-margin hits, and replacing a bedside nurse costs roughly $55-60K by industry surveys. Meanwhile office-conversion lenders will not fund without a credit tenant, and 2026 rates are punishing.
solution: A 'space-to-housing' package: a utilization audit of admin real estate (badge, Wi-Fi and parking data), floor-by-floor conversion screening, a 10-15 year staff-housing master lease structured as a recruiting and retention benefit (rent by payroll deduction), tax-exempt or community-benefit financing, and a co-development partner. Fee at financial close.
why_now: AI scribes and RCM automation went mainstream in 2025-26, and Medicaid cuts force hospitals to monetize idle assets. Office vacancy is 17.8% with $39B of office debt maturing in 12 months. Public-partnered conversions such as 100 Gold Street (4,000 units) show a mission-aligned pipeline. PE physician-practice deals are down about 50%, so systems are holding more real estate.
revenue_model: $40-90K feasibility fee, a 1-2% success fee or development-fee share at close, ongoing asset-management fees.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce ingredient in office conversion is not design but a credit tenant. A hospital is the rare mission-aligned credit with a hard-dollar reason to want housing (turnover cost), and its own back offices are the least visible vacancy on the market.
first_30_days: Build a public-data list of 30 nonprofit systems with admin campuses (IRS Schedule H, county records, satellite parking counts). Cold-pitch a free two-page 'vacancy read' to their real-estate VPs. Convert 2-3 into paid audits within 90 days.

title: Telemetry-Underwritten Credit for Defense Sub-Tier Shops
one_liner: Plug low-cost MTConnect adapters into shop CNC machines to create tamper-evident proof of utilization and surge capacity that unlocks equipment loans and rated-order credit lines, and gives primes the capacity data they lack.
customer: 10-50 person machine shops, foundries and sheet-metal shops pursuing defense work (they pay $149-299 a month). Lenders, CDFIs and equipment lessors pay origination fees, and primes and state defense-industrial-base offices later pay for verified-capacity queries.
problem: An industry study finds 'no fit-for-purpose investment model' between R&D and mature production for sub-tier suppliers (castings, forgings, sensors, rocket motors), with VC a sliver and PE putting in only $1-3B a year. Hadrian raised $1.37B while metals robot orders rose just 3% in H1, and shops cannot fund a machine or a cobot cell. Lenders underwrite job shops on tax returns and collateral, and DoD has no real-time data on free spindle-hours.
solution: A hardware-light MTConnect and OPC UA adapter kit and cloud service that logs spindle utilization, part counts, scrap and on-time delivery with signed, tamper-evident records. It issues a 'verified capacity score', lender-ready utilization letters and attestations for DPAS-rated orders, and an anonymized open-capacity feed for primes and government. Partner lenders extend equipment loans and rated-order lines against the score.
why_now: Rated orders, drone and munitions surges and Navy co-investment are pushing demand to sub-tiers just as the Navy stops funding early stages. Publicly funded defense-industrial-base lending vehicles need originators. Modern CNC controls already speak MTConnect, so the marginal hardware cost is small.
revenue_model: $149-299 a month per shop for telemetry and score, 1-2% origination fee from lenders on funded loans, and later a per-query fee from primes and agencies for verified surge capacity.
non_obvious_insight: Utilization telemetry is a better credit signal than a tax return for a job shop, and it doubles as the surge-capacity data the government has never had. The same tamper-evident record serves the lender, the prime and the auditor, so shops pay because it gets them financed.
first_30_days: Partner with a manufacturing extension center and one CDFI or equipment lessor. Install adapters on 10 machines in a defense-heavy cluster (Connecticut or Ohio) and produce the first 3 verified utilization letters to test whether a lender will price better against them.

title: Protein Allocation Co-op for Mid-Size Brands
one_liner: A buyers' co-op that pools forward volume for whey and reformulates around shortages for brands too small to get allocation.
customer: Mid-size sports-nutrition, RTD beverage and bar brands (roughly $20-200M revenue) that lack direct cheese-plant relationships.
problem: Whey isolate is around $14/lb, some suppliers are sold out through 2026, and big buyers lock allocations, so small brands pay spot prices or get nothing.
solution: Aggregate members' forward demand into direct contracts with mid-size cheese and whey processors, and run a reformulation desk that blends whey with alternative proteins to spec.
why_now: The constraint is downstream whey-processing capacity and cheese output rather than raw milk, and factories are retooling for cottage cheese, so relationships and volume commitments now decide who gets protein.
revenue_model: Annual membership plus a 2-4% margin on pooled volume and fees for the reformulation desk.
non_obvious_insight: The shortage is partly a market-structure problem for small buyers rather than an absolute supply problem. Aggregation turns a set of unattractive small accounts into one large, plannable contract.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 brands into a founding cohort with combined tonnage, then hold calls with five mid-size cheese and whey plants to test whether they will commit capacity to a pooled buyer.

title: Ticketmaster Exit Kits for Independent Venues
one_liner: A contract-audit and migration service that tells venue owners exactly when and at what cost they can leave exclusive ticketing deals, then moves them safely.
customer: Independent venue owners and operators of 500-3,000 capacity rooms in the US, and promoters who run pre-sales through those venues.
problem: A jury found Live Nation liable for illegal monopolization on 2026-04-15, and remedies remain unclear (a separate DOJ settlement dates from 2026-03-09). Venues with exclusive contracts do not know what leaving costs (liquidated damages, advance repayment, loss of fan data), and fear a botched on-sale day more than the contract.
solution: A contract analyzer that reads exclusivity, term, advance-repayment and change-of-law clauses and returns an exit date and cost sheet. Add a migration playbook (fan data export with consent, fee structure compliant with the FTC all-in rule, verified-fan pre-sales), white-label integrations with 2-3 alternative ticketing platforms, and pooled negotiation for groups of venues.
why_now: The April 2026 verdict, the FTC's all-in pricing rule (effective 2025-05-12), the state suits, and Ticketmaster's June 2026 placement inside Spotify all raise the stakes of lock-in. Venues suddenly have leverage but no capability.
revenue_model: $2-5k audit, $5-15k migration, and 10-20% of alternative platforms' fee share on the venue's tickets for three years.
non_obvious_insight: Antitrust wins create optionality, not capability. The bottleneck after a verdict is the GM's fear of a broken on-sale, so the product to sell is reduced fear, plus data ownership the venue never knew it lacked.
first_30_days: Mine the public trial exhibits for venue-contract terms and publish an exit map. Reach 10 venue GMs through independent-venue trade groups. Run three paid contract audits at $1.5k and line up two alternative ticketing partners.

title: Blinded Self-Trials for Your Supplement Stack
one_liner: Mail-order double-blind crossover kits that tell you which of your own supplements move your own labs and wearable data, and which you can stop paying for.
customer: Adults 35-65 spending $60-300 per month on vitamins, longevity stacks and nootropics. About 8 in 10 Americans take supplements, per a Pew survey published in September 2026. First reached through biohacker communities and health podcasts; later through functional-medicine and longevity practitioners who want evidence for their patients.
problem: Nobody knows whether magnesium, ashwagandha, creatine, NMN or fish oil does anything for them. Population trials show small average effects, but individual responders exist, and without blinding the placebo effect swamps everything. People keep stacks running indefinitely out of subscription inertia and spend hundreds to thousands of dollars per year with no feedback loop.
solution: The customer sends the product they already take. A partner packer or compounding pharmacist repackages it and a matched placebo into coded weekly pouches on a randomized ABAB crossover schedule with washout. Outcomes are chosen per compound: sleep and HRV from the customer's own wearable, glucose from an over-the-counter CGM (Stelo or Lingo), and fingerstick or lab draws for ApoB, hs-CRP, ferritin or vitamin D. Pre-registered Bayesian analysis returns 'keep, drop or inconclusive' with the confidence. Offered for supplements only (never prescription drugs), as self-experimentation, not medical advice. An annual 'Stack Audit' rotates one compound every six weeks.
why_now: Over-the-counter CGMs and consumer wearables now supply continuous, cheap outcome data for healthy people; fingerstick lab kits and direct-to-consumer lab ordering are cheap; supplement use is near-universal and skepticism is rising in coverage of 'mostly useless' supplements; and longevity stack culture gives buyers a natural stack to audit.
revenue_model: $129-199 per compound trial plus lab costs at cost; $349 per year Stack Audit; $60 per patient white-label for practitioners; aggregated, consented responder data licensed to academic researchers (never sold to supplement brands, to protect independence).
non_obvious_insight: The most valuable longevity product for the middle class is subtraction. The average effect of most supplements is tiny but individuals differ, and 'proven for me' is the only evidence class people trust. Unlike the industry, this business makes money when people buy less: every dropped supplement saves $20-40 per month, so the service pays for itself in months and the buyer's own spending is the marketing.
first_30_days: Recruit 40 volunteers from biohacking and supplement communities for a $49 pilot on two popular compounds (for example magnesium glycinate for sleep and creatine for energy). Have a local compounding pharmacist or contract packer prepare coded pouches and placebo. Pre-register the analysis in a public spreadsheet, run the trial, and publish an honest 'what we found, including nulls' post. Pitch five functional-medicine practices on white-labeling the kits at $60 per patient.

title: Rural Jail Pharmacy-in-a-Box for Independents
one_liner: Turn the local independent's blister packing, delivery and controlled-substance discipline into a per-inmate contract for the county jail that the sheriff is afraid of.
customer: Sheriffs, jail administrators and county commissions running jails of about 20-150 beds, whose risk pools and insurers care about medication liability. Independent pharmacies are a second customer, licensing the playbook and software.
problem: Jail medication is a sheriff's biggest lawsuit exposure: missed doses, withdrawal, wrong-inmate errors, controlled-substance counts. Small jails run it with a deputy, a clipboard and a nurse who visits two days a week. Mail-order jail pharmacies take 3-5 days, so first-night meds come from the ER or a deputy's personal trip to the drugstore. Buprenorphine and other opioid-treatment mandates funded by opioid settlements add complexity. Meanwhile local independents already run the identical workflow for nursing homes.
solution: A repeatable program with same-day intake verification (call the outside pharmacy, check the PDMP). Barcode blister-packed med pass with an offline-capable eMAR on a tablet. Controlled-substance counts with dual sign-off and photo audit. An emergency kit and a monthly consultant-pharmacist review. A 30-day bridge supply at release. Sold as a playbook, software and group-purchasing bundle so any independent can become the county's jail pharmacy, with master agreements through state association-of-counties risk pools.
why_now: Wellpath's late-2024 bankruptcy and the contract turnover that followed left counties scrambling for medical vendors. Deaths-in-custody litigation keeps rising. Opioid-settlement dollars are flowing to county jails for medication for opioid use disorder. A growing number of state Medicaid reentry waivers require medication continuity at release. Independents need any revenue line that does not depend on PBM reimbursement.
revenue_model: County per-diem or monthly retainer (roughly $1,500-6,000 a month per small jail, to be validated by state). The pharmacy pays a 10-15% platform fee plus $300-600 a month for the software. Additional revenue from risk-pool partnership programs and discharge-supply services.
non_obvious_insight: Rural jail medication is not a healthcare problem, it is a liability problem the sheriff cannot outsource to a national vendor that ships in five days. The real buyer is the county risk pool and insurer, and the independent pharmacist next door is the only entity that can deliver in thirty minutes. Small contracts often fall below county bid thresholds, and the sheriff already knows the pharmacist by first name.
first_30_days: The pharmacist calls the sheriff in their own county and offers a 60-day pilot at cost. Audit the jail's med room and write a one-page deficiency list. Propose eMAR plus packaging. Check the state pharmacy board's rules for institutional or correctional pharmacy licensure. Pitch the results to the state sheriffs' association and the county risk pool, and recruit two neighboring independents to copy the model.

title: Farm-to-Factory Water Supply Assurance
one_liner: A diligence-plus-settlement service that sells expanding plants a permit-grade, verified acre-foot supply by leasing fallowed farm water in drought-stressed Western basins.
customer: Plant developers, site-selection teams and economic-development agencies for semiconductor, pharma and food plants in AZ, TX, ID and UT. Irrigation districts and farmers are the supply side.
problem: Water is now a siting gate: Texas froze grid connections over water, the Colorado River's 2027-2036 framework forces farm cuts, and Amazon put $20M into farm conservation with no settlement layer. Factories need a legally defensible supply and 'water neutral' commitments, and farmers cannot easily sell verified savings.
solution: Start with a $15-40k water-supply diligence report (rights, drought exposure, discharge capacity, PFAS in source). Then structure and meter option-style leases with farmers, with satellite and meter verification, and issue an assurance letter usable in permitting.
why_now: The Aug 2026 Colorado River Record of Decision, 49.6% of the US in drought, and reshoring in water-intensive sectors (electronics +35%, pharma +32%, food +17% in robot orders) collide.
revenue_model: Diligence fee plus 5-8% of lease flow and a verification fee per acre-foot.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest new industrial water supply is a farmer's fallowed field, but only if someone provides the paperwork that turns it into a permit-grade asset.
first_30_days: Pick one county (for example Pinal, AZ). Sign three farmers on non-binding option terms. Sell two diligence reports to plant real-estate teams or EDCs, and recruit a water-rights attorney as an advisor.

title: Task-Shifting Engine for Tech-Led Vet Visits
one_liner: Standing-order templates, scheduling and a state-by-state supervision rules database that let clinics move routine care from vets to technicians and, soon, VPAs, without breaking practice acts.
customer: Independent clinics adopting a team-based model, multi-state clinic groups, and VPA-employing practices. Later: PIMS and telehealth vendors licensing the rules API.
problem: Vet supply is nearly flat (91,100 vets; about 3,100 openings a year) while techs are scarce (about 2 per vet versus a 4:1 ideal, with most leaving within 4 years). The team-based model is how affordable clinics reach invoices about 44% below average, yet PIMS scheduling is built around doctor visits. Nobody supplies compliant protocols for who may do what under which supervision in each state.
solution: A library of 'tech appointment' types (booster vaccines, rechecks, suture removal, senior lab draws, weight programs, dental prep) with standing orders, consent scripts and a DVM sign-off queue. A versioned rules database maps each task to state supervision levels, with alerts when boards change rules, and audit logs show who did what under whose supervision. A scheduling plug-in books the right role and length.
why_now: Colorado State is launching an MS for the new VPA license (dogs and cats, supervised, routine surgery and tests), and it has been more than a decade in the making. Roll-ups now span many states, and clinics need to raise output per DVM. AI scribes and agents are generating plans that implicitly delegate tasks.
revenue_model: $199-399 per clinic per month for templates and scheduling; $500-5K per month for rules API and multi-state groups; VPA program design consulting.
non_obvious_insight: A new professional tier shifts value to whoever holds the rules and the protocols. In human health, scope-of-practice changes (NPs, PAs) spawned decades of compliance and protocol software. Vet medicine is at the start of that curve, and the rules database is the moat while templates are the wedge.
first_30_days: With a vet-law attorney, build a matrix of 10 states by about 40 tasks from statutes and board rules. Publish a free 'Can my tech do this?' checker in vet-tech communities. Pilot the appointment templates in 5 clinics and aim to sell 3 multi-state groups on the rules feed.

title: Staffed Junk Playgrounds as Apartment Amenity
one_liner: Adventure playgrounds with loose parts, dirt, tools and trained playworkers, installed on unused lots at family-heavy apartment communities and sold to landlords as a renewal lever.
customer: Owners and operators of garden-style, suburban and build-to-rent multifamily communities (200+ units, many households with children ages 5-12). Parents are the secondary payers via optional drop-in fees.
problem: Roughly 40 states now require schools to restrict phones, yet the 3-6pm window at home is where screen time actually happens. Australia's under-16 social media ban has reportedly changed daily use only slightly (about 58% still use daily vs about 60% before), a sign that removing a device without providing somewhere to go does little. Parents want unsupervised, physical, unstructured play but fear liability and have no safe place. Meanwhile landlords spend amenity budgets on gyms and coworking rooms nobody uses and lose family tenants to turnover that costs thousands of dollars per unit.
solution: A turnkey adventure playground service in the UK 'playwork' tradition: pallets, tires, rope, cardboard, sand, water, hammers and a supervised fire pit on an old parking lot or lawn, run 15-20 hours a week (after school and weekends) by trained playworkers who intervene as little as possible. The operator supplies the loose-parts kit, a written risk-benefit assessment, staff training, a background-check protocol and a specialty liability policy. The property signs a monthly contract, and families pay nothing or a small add-on. Tracked outcomes include tenant survey scores and renewal rates for families with school-age children.
why_now: Phone-free school laws spread across about 40 states by mid-2026 and the 'anxious generation' framing turned play-based childhood into a mainstream parenting goal. Free-range parenting statutes in a growing number of states reduce neglect-law fear. Build-to-rent operators are competing on amenities and retention. Nonprofit adventure playgrounds exist but cannot scale because of staffing and liability, which a landlord-funded model solves.
revenue_model: Service contract of about $3-5k per property per month (staff, materials, insurance, management), optional $15-20 per child drop-in for non-residents, and multi-property master agreements with regional operators. Ten properties gives roughly $400-600k in annual recurring revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyer of 'screen-free childhood' is the landlord, not the parent. One prevented move-out saves thousands of dollars in turnover, so a single retained family pays for a month of the program, and kids' friendships create lock-in that no gym can. The barrier to adventure playgrounds was never demand, it was insurance and staffing, and packaging them as a managed property service turns a nonprofit hobby into infrastructure.
first_30_days: Find one friendly 300-unit community and offer an 8-week free trial in exchange for data. Spend about $2k on pallets, tires, rope and tools, hire two playwork or early-childhood students, and get a liability quote from a specialty broker. Survey tenants with kids before and after, and track leasing-team feedback. Photograph everything and pitch 20 regional property managers through local apartment associations and LinkedIn. Aim to convert the trial and one more property to paid contracts within 4-5 months.

title: A Marketplace for Canal Capacity, Not Water
one_liner: A scheduling and capacity-release board that lets irrigation districts sell idle canal and wheeling capacity so conserved or recharge water can physically move to buyers.
customer: Irrigation districts and mutual ditch companies with spare conveyance capacity (sellers), plus growers, groundwater agencies, cities and conservation buyers who need water moved (buyers). Districts pay a subscription and buyers pay per acre-foot wheeled.
problem: Everyone is building marketplaces for water rights and acre-feet. In Western practice the binding constraint is often the ability and permission to move water: capacity, wheeling agreements, losses, turnout scheduling. Idle capacity sits unused while buyers cannot get water delivered. Districts handle wheeling requests by phone and spreadsheet.
solution: Wedge: a shared capacity calendar and wheeling-request workflow for districts, with loss accounting and standard agreements. Then a capacity-release market, like the gas-pipeline capacity release model. The ditch-company share ledger (shares, assessments, transfer approvals) is phase two. Start with one region where transfers already happen.
why_now: The 2027-2036 Colorado River framework and corporate buyers like Amazon create conserved water that must be moved. California groundwater rules and canal capacity loss to subsidence make wheeling scarce. Cheap LoRa gate sensors and open flow gauges make district digitization affordable.
revenue_model: $10-40k/yr district SaaS, plus $5-15 per acre-foot wheeled (roughly 3-5% of price).
non_obvious_insight: Price discovery is missing for the pipes, not the water. Whoever runs the capacity ledger sees every buyer, seller and route, and that data is the moat for every later water market product.
first_30_days: Interview 10 district managers and ditch riders and find one that handles recurring wheeling requests manually. Ship a free shared calendar and request workflow to that district using off-the-shelf tools. Agree that the district will pay per wheeled acre-foot at season end. Publish a public canal-capacity map from open gauge data as top-of-funnel.

title: Liquidity for Managers of Overheld PE Companies
one_liner: Give executives in stuck PE portfolio companies a way to cash out part of their vested equity through third-party buyers, so sponsors can fix management retention without diluting the fund or forcing an exit.
customer: Lower-middle-market PE sponsors and independent sponsors holding 2019-2021 vintage platforms. They pay for the diagnostic. Portfolio-company CEOs, CFOs and operators hold vested profits interests or options. Family offices and secondary funds supply the capital that buys management equity.
problem: Hold periods have stretched to roughly seven years. Management teams are fatigued and their incentive plans have lost value, which raises the risk they leave. The fund cannot exit (LPs tolerate little markdown), and topping up the management incentive plan (MIP) dilutes the sponsor's remaining upside.
solution: (1) A 'MIP Health Check': a waterfall model built from the operating agreement showing each manager's equity value under three exit dates and prices, with a retention-risk score. (2) A 'management tender desk': arrange third-party purchase of 10-25% of a manager's vested units at a negotiated discount, with sponsor consent and rights of first refusal, funded by a syndicate of family offices and secondary funds. (3) A cost and dilution comparison against a traditional MIP reload. Structured through a registered broker-dealer partner and securities counsel.
why_now: Bain's 2026 midyear report says most buyout assets were acquired in 2021 or earlier, the implied capital cycle is about seven years, and roughly one in five LPs are cutting buyout allocations. Bain's year-end outlook counts 32,000 unrealized companies worth $3.8T and says 40% of portfolio companies are held over 5 years, versus 29% in 2019. Fund-level returns flatten after year eight, so the pressure to retain operators through the extended hold is acute.
revenue_model: $5-10K per MIP Health Check billed to the sponsor. 1.5-3% placement fee on tender volume, paid by buyers. Later, SaaS for waterfall tracking at $1-3K/month per fund.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is human capital inside assets that cannot be sold, and the only retention lever that costs the fund nothing in dilution is third-party liquidity for managers. Bain's midyear report says: 'Stretched holding periods have fatigued management teams and depleted incentive plan value, complicating mid-hold value-creation refreshes,' and that more than half of LPs cap tolerated markdowns on full exits at 5%, which pushes GPs to hold underperformers longer (https://www.bain.com/insights/private-equity-midyear-report-2026/). 'Stretched holds' and '12 is the new 5' EBITDA growth targets (https://www.bain.com/insights/welcome-to-a-new-era-global-private-equity-report-2026/) mean operators are being asked to deliver more for longer. Employee tender offers are routine in venture-backed startups but are, by my inference, rare for PE-backed profits interests, so this looks like an open niche. That is an inference from the sources, not something they state. Regulatory structure is the main risk.
first_30_days: Build a profits-interest waterfall calculator from a standard operating-agreement template. Retain securities and tax counsel for a scoping memo and line up a registered broker-dealer partner. Offer free Health Checks to 15 independent sponsors and lower-mid-market GPs with 2019-2021 vintage assets, reached through ACG, Searchfunder and direct outreach. Then sign 2-3 paid checks at $5K and use the results to pitch one family office to fund a first tender.

title: Estate Planning for People's AI Agents
one_liner: Powers of attorney, dead-man switches and revocation tooling for the agents that hold standing authority over your money, email and subscriptions.
customer: Estate-planning attorneys and RIAs or family offices serving tech founders and executives who already run personal agents, followed by consumers through those channels.
problem: Personal agents now hold standing authority: card mandates, wallets, email access, autopay and negotiations. Step two: authority is tied to a living principal. Step three: death, incapacity, divorce or bankruptcy leaves agents acting on stale instructions or locks heirs out. Fiduciary access laws (for example RUFADAA) give no automatic access to digital accounts, and nobody has drafted for delegated software.
solution: An Agent Schedule for estate plans. It combines an inventory of agents, OAuth grants, wallets and mandates (via connectors), attorney-drafted clauses giving a digital fiduciary authority to pause, transfer or delete agents and limiting post-death actions, an incapacity or dead-man trigger that rotates credentials and downgrades permissions to read-only while notifying the fiduciary, and export of agent memory and logs for the executor.
why_now: Personal agents went mainstream in 2026 (OpenClaw reached about 247k GitHub stars), and agentic wallets and machine-payment rails launched in February and March 2026. The estate bar is only starting to publish AI afterlife primers, and they focus on AI personas, not delegated agents.
revenue_model: $500-$1,500 per client schedule sold through attorneys (roughly $300 wholesale), $10-$30/month monitoring, and $5k/year RIA channel licenses.
non_obvious_insight: Every technology that received delegated authority (checks, credit cards, cloud accounts) eventually got a legal instrument for the case where the principal stops existing. Agents have none yet, and the trigger events are guaranteed, so demand arrives on a calendar.
first_30_days: Draft the template with 2 estate attorneys. Pilot with 10 founders through an existing network. Build a simple inventory and revocation checklist using OAuth grant discovery for Google, Microsoft 365, GitHub and 5 agent platforms, and charge $750 per pilot.

title: Memory Budget CI for Game Studios
one_liner: CI tooling and fixed-fee audits that enforce RAM and VRAM budgets per target device, because the assumption that hardware gets better each generation just broke.
customer: Mid-size PC and console studios (30-300 staff) shipping in 2027 to Steam Deck, Switch 2 and 8-16GB PCs.
problem: AI data centers are absorbing the RAM supply. Valve's Steam Machine launched at $1,049 against an early target of about $800, Xbox prices rose, and Switch 2 goes to $499.99 on 2026-09-01. The installed base will stay at today's memory ceilings for years, but studios budget memory as a fixed cap and find regressions in late QA.
solution: An Unreal, Unity and Godot CI plugin that builds against device memory profiles, snapshots per-level memory, attributes growth to specific assets and pull requests, and suggests fixes (texture format changes, streaming pool sizes, audio bank downsampling). Sold alongside a 3-week 'memory diet' audit that finds duplicated and unstripped assets.
why_now: Memory vendors now quote a monthly price and a yes-or-no on volume, per a Valve engineer. Console and handheld price hikes in 2026 mean players will not upgrade into new game requirements. Studios are planning holiday 2026-27 lineups now.
revenue_model: $15-40k per audit, $400-2,500 per month per studio for CI, and later a subscription to a device-profile and min-spec benchmark database.
non_obvious_insight: The industry's optimization culture is about frame time. When hardware gets pricier over its life, the cheapest way to grow the addressable market is to shrink footprint, and most footprint is asset-pipeline waste that can be found and fixed automatically.
first_30_days: Publish an analysis of Steam minimum-spec trends versus the Hardware Survey to get inbound. Ship a free open-source memory snapshot diff tool for Unity and Unreal. Offer free audits to 5 studios in exchange for case studies, and convert 2 into paid engagements.

title: Assay-Verified Swarf Pooling for Machine Shops
one_liner: Turn the chip bin into a revenue line: two-bin alloy segregation, assayed weekly pickup, and pooled truckloads sold direct to mills and remelters.
customer: Ohio job shops and mid-size plants (20-300 employees) machining stainless, nickel alloys, titanium, brass or tool steel, especially aerospace, energy and medical suppliers. The first buyer is the plant manager or owner. A second buyer is any prime or OEM that wants a closed-loop 'revert' chain-of-custody.
problem: The chip bin is the only place in a shop where money leaves blind. Most shops tip all chips into one roll-off. The scrap yard grades by eye or its own XRF and pays a mixed-lot price. One shovel of aluminum in 316 stainless, or too much cutting oil, can drop the price by 30%-70%, while clean, segregated titanium and nickel-alloy turnings sell at multiples of mixed scrap. Nobody at the shop has time to sort, and small volumes are too tiny for mills to accept directly.
solution: 'SwarfStack': color-coded, RFID-tagged two- and three-bin systems in the shop, plus a weekly route truck with an onboard scale and a handheld XRF that assays each pickup and logs photo, weight, alloy and oil content to a shared ledger. A centrifuge or briquetter handles the oil. Pool by alloy across dozens of shops into full truckloads sold directly to mills, foundries and remelters. Pay the shop 70%-80% of net price and issue a digital scrap certificate for chain-of-custody. The provenance data becomes more valuable as metals tariffs increasingly reward proof of where metal was melted.
why_now: Reshoring is adding domestic machining hours, and with them chips. Metals lead times and alloy volatility keep prices high. The April 2026 Section 232 rewrite taxes the full customs value of metal derivatives and gives better treatment to U.S.-melted content, so provenance now has a price. Used handheld XRF analyzers now cost about what a used pickup does, and cheap vision models can identify alloy family from a photo of a bin.
revenue_model: A 20%-30% spread between the pooled sale price and what the shop is paid, plus $150-$300 per month bin and route fees, plus a small fee per digital scrap certificate. A route with 60 shops averaging $1,500 per month of chip value nets about $250k-$400k per year, before adding a briquetting and coolant-recovery arm.
non_obvious_insight: The scrap dealer's edge is not market power, it is that the shop does not know what is in its own bin. The metal was worth far more than the 'mixed' price, and shops give away five-figure sums each year without ever seeing the invoice line.
first_30_days: Buy a used handheld XRF for about $15k-$25k and rent a pickup with a platform scale. Sign 8 aerospace and medical suppliers in one county, starting with those cutting titanium, Inconel or stainless. Run pickups, assay each load, and send each shop a 'you left $X in your bin' statement showing the uplift against their current dealer. Pre-sell pooled loads to one stainless remelter and one titanium remelter before the first truckload.

title: Payer Offset and Recoupment Radar
one_liner: Reconstruct the silent payer clawbacks buried in the 835 provider-level adjustment segment, then dispute the ones that lack notice or exceed state look-back limits.
customer: Community and mid-size hospitals, physician groups and MSOs, and RCM outsourcers who want a recovery line item. SaaS at $1-3k/month, or 15-25% of reversed recoupments.
problem: Payers increasingly claw money back by netting it inside the electronic remittance (835) PLB provider-level balance segment, or by short-paying unrelated claims. These adjustments carry cryptic reason codes and no patient or claim detail. Cash posters drop them into a suspense or 'other adjustment' account, or write them off. The overpayment letters that justify them arrive by mail, fax or random emails and are never matched. Many states cap retroactive recoupment look-back windows and require claim-level notice, but no one checks whether the payer complied.
solution: Ingest 12-24 months of 835s and the payer's overpayment and audit letters (PDF/email/fax OCR). Rebuild every offset to claim level. Flag recoupments with no valid notice, past the state or contract look-back, duplicating a prior recoupment, or hitting claims already appealed. Generate dispute letters and track outcomes. A payer scorecard shows clawback dollars per $1M paid, which gives the CFO leverage at contract renewal.
why_now: Payer payment-integrity programs are scaling with AI-driven post-payment audits and coding-policy downcodes. Medicare Advantage audit pressure is rising. Hospitals staffed thin after the 2025-26 Medicaid and margin squeeze cannot chase each offset by hand. Post-payment recoupment is the fastest-growing part of the denial problem and the least instrumented.
revenue_model: Contingency 15-25% of recoupments reversed, or $1-3k/month per facility for monitoring plus a $5-10k onboarding audit. Payer scorecards can be sold to hospital associations.
non_obvious_insight: Denial management tools watch denied claims. Recoupments are not denied claims. They are negative dollars in the remit file that nobody owns. Only cash posters see them and they are told to just post them. In a typical mid-size hospital these unmatched offsets total mid-six to seven figures a year, and dispute success is highest exactly where the payer skipped required notice. The data is already sitting in files the hospital owns.
first_30_days: Ask 5 friendly hospital and group cash-posting managers for 12 months of 835s (clearinghouses can export them), which requires only a BAA. Write a parser for the PLB segments (about a week of work) and produce a 'recoupment leakage report' showing unmatched offset dollars per payer. Use the number to sign 2 contingency pilots, and build the letter-matching module on real customer data.

title: Rent Ledger for Adult Kids Living at Home
one_liner: A simple lease, payment and credit-reporting layer that lets parents charge their adult children rent, build the kids' credit history, and quietly bank the money as a down-payment fund.
customer: Parents (Gen X and Boomers) with adult children aged 22-30 living at home, paying $12/month per household. Secondary revenue from mortgage lenders and first-time-buyer programs.
problem: Nearly half (49%) of US adults under 30 lived with parents in 2025, up 12 percentage points from 2019 (Federal Reserve SHED). Only 63% of adults could cover a $400 emergency with cash or a paid-off card, and the Fed reports 16% of adults use buy-now-pay-later, with 11% of users hit by overdraft fees from missed payments. Lender-side data shows BNPL is spreading into groceries (a LendingTree survey reported nearly a quarter of BNPL users financed groceries, up from 14%; 41% reported a late payment). These young adults are paying for hobbies, subscriptions and installment plans while accruing no rent history at all, since informal family housing builds no credit and no savings discipline.
solution: An app that produces a simple parent-child lease, collects a modest monthly 'rent' by ACH, reports on-time payments to the credit bureaus through an established rent-reporting partner (do not become a furnisher), and lets the parent choose to escrow the money in a labeled account toward a future down payment or move-out fund. It gives the kid a monthly statement and a BNPL and subscription view so obligations don't collide with rent day. It includes parent-side documentation of the rent for tax purposes (tax treatment is a gray area, so it needs CPA-reviewed templates).
why_now: The 12-point jump in under-30s living at home is now structural, not a pandemic blip. Rent reporting has been mainstreamed by consumer fintechs and by underwriting systems that count rental payment history, and BNPL late payments are rising, which raises the value of a credibility-building habit. Housing costs make first-time down payments the main goal for these households.
revenue_model: $12/month per household (parent pays), $5/month optional kid add-on for credit-builder features. Referral fees from mortgage lenders and down-payment-assistance programs when the kid buys. Later: employer benefit channel for parents.
non_obvious_insight: Parents are the largest unpriced landlord class in the US, and they already hold the leverage the market lacks: the kid will pay them and will not skip. The product isn't a rent app, it is a behavioral bridge that converts a free-rent arrangement into credit history plus parent-held savings. Evidence: Federal Reserve SHED 2025 https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2026-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2025-executive-summary.htm (49% of under-30s living with parents, +12 points since 2019; 63% cover $400; 16% BNPL, 11% overdraft fees) and BNPL grocery and late-payment figures via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buy_now,_pay_later (summarizing LendingTree). Assumptions to validate first: that bureaus and lenders will accept rent reported for a parent-landlord and how underwriting treats it, and that parents want to charge rent and save it. I found no survey on either.
first_30_days: Interview 20 parents in local parenting and finance Facebook groups. Test a landing page and a $12/month waitlist. Run a concierge pilot with 10 families: a lease template, ACH collection, an existing rent-reporting partner and a shared spreadsheet. Confirm with a mortgage broker whether reported parent-landlord rent helps underwriting. Target 15 paying families and one lender-partner conversation.

title: Death Certificate Sign-Off Copilot for Hospices
one_liner: Get physicians to complete valid cause-of-death certifications in hours instead of days, sold to the hospices and care groups that get blamed for the delay, with funeral homes as the free wedge.
customer: Hospice organizations and nursing-home or assisted-living groups. The buyer is the VP of operations or hospice medical director, motivated by family-experience scores and clinician time. Funeral homes use a free version that seeds the data.
problem: Nothing moves until a physician completes the medical section of the death certificate in the state's electronic system. Cremation authorization, burial permits and certified copies for the family all wait. Doctors forget logins, delegate poorly, or enter invalid cause-of-death chains such as 'cardiac arrest', which triggers rejections or medical examiner referrals. A funeral director spends hours per case chasing certifiers, families see the delay as the funeral home's fault, and the cooler fills up while everyone waits.
solution: Phase one is a free web and text tool for funeral homes. They log each pending certificate, and the tool sends the certifier a one-tap reminder with clear instructions and shows a status page. Phase two is the paid hospice product: from the discharge summary or chart export, an AI drafts the Part I/Part II cause-of-death chain in line with NCHS conventions, flags ME-reportable triggers before submission, and routes a mobile magic-link for physician review. In states that allow certifier designees, hospice staff do the data entry. A dashboard shows time-to-certify by physician and site, with escalation rules.
why_now: Electronic death registration systems are now near-universal, so a digital workflow is possible. LLMs can reliably summarize a chart for physician review in a way that wasn't safe or cheap a few years ago. Hospice growth and public CAHPS Hospice scores raise the stakes of family experience. Medical director workloads are rising with physician shortages.
revenue_model: $35-$60 per certificate processed, or $200-$500/month per hospice site plus per-certifier seats. Optional $99/month funeral-home tier with analytics and multi-hospice benchmarking. Later, sell the anonymized time-to-certify benchmark to hospice chains and payers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone blames the funeral home for slowness, but we spend more time chasing doctors than doing the actual work. This 'post-death workflow orphan' sits after the patient leaves the EHR workflow, so no health-tech vendor sees it. The funeral home is the only party who measures days-from-death-to-certificate. So sell backwards: give funeral homes a free chase tool, collect the scorecard on which hospices and doctors are slow, then walk into those hospices with their own numbers.
first_30_days: Build the no-PHI funeral-home chase tool (case ID, certifier name and phone, state) in two weeks. Recruit 15 funeral homes in two states through the state association. After 60 days publish an anonymized 'days-to-certify by hospice' scorecard. Book meetings with the three slowest hospices and offer a $2,000/month pilot with a signed BAA. Have a physician advisor review the cause-of-death logic.

title: GLP-1 Menu Labeling Layer for Independent Restaurants
one_liner: A cheap per-dish protein, fiber and portion labeling and half-portion pricing tool that tells the 12% of diners on GLP-1 drugs which dishes fit, published wherever they look.
customer: Owner-operated independent restaurants and small groups (2-30 locations), plus campus and hospital cafeterias, that sell through delivery apps and Google Maps. They pay $199 setup and $39/month.
problem: About 11-12% of US adults now take GLP-1 drugs, up from 3% in 2024 (KFF poll). Chains have reacted with lighter-portion sections, protein menus and dedicated GLP-1 menus (Olive Garden, Shake Shack, Chipotle, Subway, Smoothie King). Independents have no dietitian, no nutrition data and no way to show which dishes fit. Their menus say nothing about protein grams or half sizes, and independents are exempt from chain menu-labeling rules.
solution: The owner uploads a menu PDF or photo. The tool estimates per-dish calories, protein and fiber as a range, using LLM recipe parsing plus USDA FoodData Central. It tags dishes 'protein-first' or 'light plate' using explicit, published thresholds. It suggests a half-portion or 'box half before it reaches the table' price point that keeps margin (food cost is typically about 30% of price, so a half portion at 65-70% of price holds gross profit). It then auto-publishes to the Google Business Profile menu, DoorDash and Uber Eats descriptions, a QR menu and printable table tents, with a short staff script. All output is worded as an estimate with no medical claims.
why_now: Health-topic search data shows GLP1 at 1.5M monthly searches (+1,011%) and Fibremaxxing +7,900%, and Google's Summergeist report shows fibermaxxing at an all-time high. Chains are now marketing to this group in 2026, so independents are losing a segment that dines out often.
revenue_model: $199 setup, $39/month per location for menu updates, delivery-app syncing and 'reorder tag' analytics. Add-ons: $99 printed table tents and $149 chef-recipe reformulation consult. Later: bundle through POS resellers, delivery-marketing agencies and restaurant associations.
non_obvious_insight: The gap is communication, not the menu. A 2026 survey cited by ABC News found 89% of GLP-1 users wish restaurants 'communicated better about options that promote health and wellness' while 90% say restaurants typically do offer healthy items. The same coverage cites a National Restaurant Association survey that GLP-1 users make 7.6 restaurant purchases a week versus 5.1 for non-users. They want 'half-sized and lunch-sized portions, protein-first options... the ability to box food before it reaches the table' (https://abcnews.com/US/weight-loss-drug-usage-grows-restaurants-offer-glp/story?id=135711648). So the cheapest fix is labeling and relabeling what a kitchen already makes, not building new dishes, and nutrition-lab analysis is unnecessary. Chain moves are documented at https://www.foodingredientsfirst.com/news/glp-1-friendly-menus-food-dining-2026.html and https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/smaller-portions-protein-glp-1s-are-quietly-changing-chain-restaurant-rcna254178, which both say nothing about independents, so that segment is unserved. Search demand: https://explodingtopics.com/health-topics.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: build the menu parser, estimates and tag thresholds, and have a registered dietitian review the method and disclaimers. Days 8-20: walk into 30 independent restaurants in one dense neighborhood with a free 'GLP-1 menu scorecard' on their own menu, and pitch via the local restaurant association and Toast/Square consultants. Days 21-30: onboard 8-10 paying restaurants, publish updated Google Business Profile and delivery listings, and track half-portion attach rate and new-visitor searches for a case study.

title: Trust Oracle for Rental Listings and Agents
one_liner: An API that answers whether a vacation rental exists, is legally registered and is controlled by the host, so payment firms, insurers and AI booking agents can refuse scams.
customer: Payment providers handling travel, travel insurers, villa-rental agencies and AI trip-agent developers, later consumers via a plug-in.
problem: AI-generated photos and cloned listings fuel rental fraud, and agents will soon book unattended. The EU short-term rental regulation requires registration numbers from May 2026, but there is no cross-border way to verify them and each registry differs. Bans (Barcelona 2028, Palma) will also see illegal listings delisted at the last minute, stranding guests.
solution: Aggregate public registries (Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, France, NYC and others), geocode the address and match it to satellite and street imagery, reverse-search photos and detect duplicates. Return a verified, unverified or unregistered verdict with evidence in under two seconds, as an API and an agent tool.
why_now: Registry numbers make 'is it legal' a lookup for the first time, agentic booking needs automated trust, and AI imagery has broken manual checks. Enforcement is rising (Spain's USD 75M fine on Airbnb).
revenue_model: USD 0.05-0.50 per check, USD 2-10K per month enterprise plans, and a share of insurer premiums saved.
non_obvious_insight: Registration numbers convert legality from opinion into data, and agents cannot get a bad feeling about a listing. Whoever builds the legality and fraud graph first becomes infrastructure for every automated booking flow.
first_30_days: Build for Spain, Italy and Portugal using public registers. Offer a free check widget to villa agencies, and backtest known scam cases to pitch two travel-insurer fraud teams.

title: Blue UAS Bill-of-Materials Origin Auditor
one_liner: Part-by-part origin verification so 60,000-drone orders do not fail on hidden Chinese-origin motors, radios and cameras.
customer: Drone makers and their integrators selling to DoD and public safety, and the primes that must certify their subcontractors' parts.
problem: Compliance requires proving that components meet domestic-content and ownership rules, but sub-tier motors, ESCs, batteries and cameras often trace to opaque distributors. Manufacturers self-certify with spreadsheets and hope a re-labelled part is not found mid-contract.
solution: Upload a BOM and receive origin confidence per part. Cross-check import records, distributor invoices, factory databases and optional lab teardown or spectrum fingerprinting of sample units. Deliver an auditor-ready dossier and alerts when a supplier changes source.
why_now: Drone Dominance orders make component provenance a gating item for tens of thousands of units. About 48 defense firms are IPO candidates and want clean compliance records. Gauntlet winners must scale quickly and can't afford a failed audit (verify statutory citations).
revenue_model: $5-25K per BOM audit, $2-8K per month for monitoring, and per-sample teardown fees.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not certification but suppliers' unofficial data. Trade-data analytics plus teardown labs beat legal-only compliance firms because they can catch a repackaged part.
first_30_days: Audit 3 drone BOMs for free to build a dataset. Hire a customs-data analyst and a contract RF engineer. Pitch Gauntlet participants directly.
